Answers sit directly under each part, hidden. Click Show answer only after you have said your full reasoning aloud for that part. Check (a) before you start (b), that is the point of the layout.

Rate your confidence before every reveal. A dashed line sits above each answer block. Say high, medium or guessed out loud before you click. A right answer said hesitantly stays ACTIVE; a right answer said confidently moves on.

Every question below is a real exam paper question. The stem is the paper's own wording, and the paper, year and question number are named in the Sources block at the foot of every question. Where a stem has been edited it is only so that it stands without the parts of the original that came before it, and the edit is written out in that same block.

Nine questions, 78 marks, 24 parts. The set is sized for coverage, not for the clock. Questions 1 to 4 are the bacterial cell, the prokaryotic genome and binary fission, 33 marks; questions 5 to 9 are horizontal gene transfer and the cell theory, 45 marks.

This is the cluster the specimen actually tested. Question 2 is the whole of 9477 Specimen Paper 3 Question 1(a), all three parts, at its real 6 marks. That was the only place Book 4 appeared on Paper 3, and the outcome it tested was 2(d), the prokaryote against eukaryote genome comparison, which neither chapter of your notes builds in one place. Part (c) is endosymbiosis, a word with zero hits anywhere in the 9477 syllabus, described in plain language and worth two marks.

The other anchors. Question 3 is HCI's own 2021 Paper 3 Section B essay at its real 10 marks, and it is the full-cycle question: binary fission end to end, plus a comparison with mitosis. Question 8 is ACJC's 2023 Paper 3 Section B essay at its real 14 marks, and it is the cumulative one: it needs the whole of Cluster 1's cell-theory argument and adds prokaryotes and eukaryotes to it.

Three real figures. Every figure is the real image from the paper the question came from, not a redrawing. One further figure could not be recovered from its paper; that part carries the paper's own description as prose instead, and says so.

No read-off-the-graph parts. There is no graph in this drill. The three figures are stimulus for an identify, an explain and an experimental deduction.

Two MCQs, both real, both audited. Question 4(c) is 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Question 12, whose key is genuinely contested, so the scheme argues both readings rather than pretending one is settled. Question 9(b) is a four-row table where every row has to be checked against all three processes.

What the marks reward. The cells are F+ and F-, and a scheme prints (REJECT DONOR) and (REJECT RECIPIENT). The sex pilus makes contact and retracts; the cytoplasmic mating bridge carries the DNA. What is transferred is the F plasmid, with plasmid and F+ plasmid both rejected. In transformation it is fragments of naked DNA, with chromosomal DNA rejected as too big. In binary fission the cell membrane invaginates, with cell wall invaginates rejected. Pair virulent and lytic with generalised and temperate and lysogenic with specialised. State the benefit as gaining advantageous genes, and say genetic variation, not diversity. Add the rolling circle mechanism and the origin of transfer to any conjugation answer: eight or more prelim schemes credit them and your chapter contains neither.

Conjugation transfers the F plasmid and only the F plasmid, and that is a complete answer.

Question 1 [7 marks]

Fig. 1.1 shows the arrangement of the bacterial chromosome and a plasmid in a bacterial cell.

(a) An example of a plasmid is the F plasmid. The F plasmid is involved in conjugation. State two ways in which a plasmid such as the F plasmid differs from the bacterial chromosome. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) State two ways in which a plasmid such as the F plasmid differs from the bacterial chromosome. [2]

1. Any two of the following contrasts, each stated for both the bacterial chromosome and the plasmid.

2. Relative number of genes and genome size. The bacterial chromosome has a bigger genome, that is more genes, while the plasmid has a smaller genome, that is fewer genes.

3. General function of the genes. The bacterial chromosome's genes are essential for survival, for example enzymes for cell metabolism, or for the synthesis of amino acids such as tryptophan, while the plasmid's genes are not essential for survival but code for advantageous traits, for example antibiotic resistance such as ampicillin resistance.

4. Number per cell. There is only 1 bacterial chromosome, while there may be none, 1 copy, or many plasmids.

5. A further credited point elsewhere in the papers: the plasmid is capable of replication independent of the bacterial chromosome since it possesses its own origin of replication.

(b) Streptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterium normally present in the nose and throat of healthy individuals. However, it can cause serious diseases such as pneumonia and bacterial meningitis. Describe how the bacterial DNA is packaged to fit into the nucleoid region of a S. pneumoniae cell. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Describe how the bacterial DNA is packaged to fit into the nucleoid region of a S. pneumoniae cell. [2]

1. Circular double-stranded DNA molecule associated with a small amount of non-histone proteins.

2. The associated non-histone proteins cause the DNA to coil tightly to form loop domains,

3. and subsequently supercoil to form condensed DNA, that is the bacterial chromosome.

4. LO 2(d) names packing of DNA by word, so histone-like proteins, looped domains and supercoiling are required even though none of those three words appears anywhere in the syllabus. You will not be handed them in a stem.

(c) Outline the features found within a typical bacterium cell that distinguishes it from a typical plant cell. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Outline the features found within a typical bacterium cell that distinguishes it from a typical plant cell. [3]

1. Reference to lack of membrane-bound organelles in bacteria against presence of such organelles in plant cells.

2. Reference to bacterial cells containing circular DNA against plant cells containing linear DNA.

3. Reference to DNA of bacterial cells found in the nucleoid region against DNA in plant cells found in the nucleus.

4. Reference to bacterial cells containing 70S ribosomes against plant cells containing 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

5. Reference to bacterial cells containing plasmids, that is extra-chromosomal DNA, which are absent in plant cells.

6. Any other valid point. Maximum 3.

7. Reject: comparisons involving cell wall and flagella. Ignore: comparisons involving chloroplasts, vacuoles, mitochondria and so on. Read the stem before choosing axes, because this scheme narrows the ground and rejects two of the features LO 1(d) itself names.

Sources & concepts

Source: ASRJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q7(a), stem, Fig. 7.1 and key verbatim (a), renumbered Fig. 1.1; YIJC Prelim 2021 P2 Q4(a), reprinted as HCI Topical 2021 STQ Q16(a), stem and key verbatim (b); SRJC Prelim 2018 P3 Q1(a), stem and key verbatim including both the reject and the ignore lines (c). The Fig. 1.1 image is the real Fig. 7.1 from the ASRJC 2025 Paper 2 question paper. Archetype: recall, state and describe. All three parts can be asked cold, and all three are answered from the five features LO 1(d) names plus the two credited extras. Trap: giving the plasmid difference one-sidedly, for example "plasmids are small", instead of stating both; treating the packing question as a chromosome question and describing histones and nucleosomes, which are eukaryotic; offering the cell wall or the flagellum in (c), which that scheme rejects by name even though LO 1(d) names the peptidoglycan cell wall; forgetting that the nucleoid is a region and not a compartment, so there is no envelope and no pore. LOs: 1(d) the structure of a typical bacterial cell, in (a) and (c); 2(d) the structure and organisation of prokaryotic genomes, specifically circularity, packing of DNA and extrachromosomal DNA, in (a), (b) and (c). Reach-back to Book 1 for plant cell ultrastructure in (c). Concepts fused: (1) plasmid against chromosome on gene number; (2) essential against non-essential genes; (3) copy number per cell; (4) independent replication from its own origin; (5) non-histone proteins as the packing agent; (6) looped domains; (7) supercoiling; (8) absence of membrane-bound organelles; (9) circular against linear DNA; (10) nucleoid against nucleus; (11) 70S against 80S ribosomes; (12) plasmids as a feature eukaryotes lack.

Question 2 [8 marks]

In 1987, Cann, Stoneking and Wilson published the suggestion that all modern humans are descended from one woman, who became known as Mitochondrial Eve. Their suggestion was based on the analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). mtDNA is circular and contains 37 genes. Mitochondria are only found in eukaryotic cells but mtDNA shares similarities with the genomes of prokaryotes.

(a) State one way in which a typical prokaryotic genome and a typical eukaryotic genome are similar. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) State one way in which a typical prokaryotic genome and a typical eukaryotic genome are similar. [1] [INFERRED: the 9477 specimen papers ship without a mark scheme; cross-checked against SAJC Prelim 2024 P3 Q2(c) and MI Prelim 2017 P2 Q9(a), whose keys give the same axes]

1. Both genomes are double-stranded DNA.

2. Or both contain genes coding for proteins.

3. The command word is state on a one-mark part, so one clause and nothing developed. This is the mark most often thrown away, because candidates look for a difference by reflex.

(b) List three ways in which a typical prokaryotic genome and a typical eukaryotic genome are different. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) List three ways in which a typical prokaryotic genome and a typical eukaryotic genome are different. [3] [INFERRED: no official key; axes taken from the outcome's own wording and cross-checked against MI Prelim 2017 P2 Q9(a)]

1. Any three of the following, each as one line. The command word is list, so three one-line statements and nothing developed.

2. Circular against linear.

3. A single chromosome, plus plasmids, against many chromosomes.

4. Held in a nucleoid with no nuclear envelope, against enclosed in a nucleus by a nuclear envelope.

5. Packed by histone-like proteins into looped domains and supercoiled, against packed by histones into nucleosomes and chromatin.

6. Introns absent, so no splicing is required, against introns present, so splicing is required.

7. Plasmids present against plasmids absent.

8. Smaller genome, that is fewer nucleotides, against larger genome with a higher proportion of non-coding DNA.

(c) Scientists have suggested that mitochondria may have originated as independent, free-living prokaryotic cells that became engulfed by primitive eukaryotic cells in a process similar to endocytosis. These cells continued to function inside the cells that had engulfed them. Describe two features of mitochondria that provide support for any parts of this hypothesis. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Describe two features of mitochondria that provide support for any parts of this hypothesis. [2] [INFERRED: no official key; the five lines of evidence below are the school's own list]

1. Mitochondria contain circular DNA which is not associated with histones, resembling the chromosomes of bacteria.

2. Ribosomes of mitochondria are more similar to prokaryotic ribosomes in size, RNA sequences and sensitivity to antibiotics than to the eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes, that is 70S against 80S.

3. Mitochondria replicate by a splitting process similar to certain prokaryotes, which is binary fission by another name.

4. Mitochondria possess cellular machinery, including ribosomes, needed to transcribe and translate their DNA into proteins.

5. The inner membrane has enzymes and transport systems similar to those found in the plasma membranes of living prokaryotes.

6. A sixth answer the chapter does not list, and the cheapest one available on a stem that itself names endocytosis: an organelle engulfed by endocytosis ends up wrapped in an inner membrane of its own plus an outer membrane derived from the host's cell surface membrane, which is exactly what a mitochondrion has. The double membrane and the circular DNA are the two safest picks.

7. The word endosymbiosis appears nowhere in the 9477 syllabus and nowhere in the specimen. You need the evidence and you never need the label.

(d) Human diseases can be caused by many different types of organisms, such as bacteria and viruses. State two differences between the genetic material of bacteria and viruses. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) State two differences between the genetic material of bacteria and viruses. [2]

1. Bacteria have DNA as their genome while viruses have either DNA or RNA as their genome.

2. Bacteria have double-stranded DNA as genetic material while viruses have either single-stranded or double-stranded nucleic acids as genetic material.

3. Bacteria have circular genetic material while viruses have linear genetic material.

4. Bacteria may have plasmids while viruses do not have plasmids.

Source: 9477 Specimen Paper 3 Question 1(a)(i), (ii) and (iii) in full, verbatim from the official question paper, at their real 1, 3 and 2 marks, with the paper's own preamble on Mitochondrial Eve condensed into the stem (a), (b) and (c). The specimen ships without a mark scheme, so every marking point is inferred and cross-checked against the school keys named above. EJC Prelim 2018 P3 Q1(a), stem and key verbatim (d). Archetype: compare and distinguish, and the only place Book 4 surfaced on the specimen's Paper 3. Note what the specimen actually asked: not the reproductive cycles and not antigenic variation, but LO 2(d) as a prokaryote-against-eukaryote comparison. Trap: losing the similarity mark in (a) by giving a difference; developing the three differences in (b) into paragraphs when the command word is list; answering (c) with "mitochondria have DNA", which does not distinguish them from a nucleus, instead of circular DNA not associated with histones; forgetting in (d) that the virus column has to be stated as an either-or, because the whole point of the viral genome is that it varies. LOs: 2(d) the structure and organisation of viral, prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes, in (a), (b), (c) and (d); 1(d) the structure of a typical bacterial cell, specifically circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, in (c). Reach-back to Cluster 1 for the viral genome in (d) and to Book 2 for histones, nucleosomes, introns and splicing in (b). Question 3 [10 marks]

(a) Prokaryotes differ from eukaryotes in terms of cell structure, genome organisation and cellular processes. Outline the mechanism of asexual reproduction by binary fission in a typical bacterial cell and compare this with the mechanism of mitosis in a eukaryotic cell. [10]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Outline the mechanism of asexual reproduction by binary fission in a typical bacterial cell and compare this with the mechanism of mitosis in a eukaryotic cell. [10]

Binary fission

1. Reference to the bacterial chromosome being attached to the cell surface membrane.

2. Reference to semi-conservative DNA replication.

3. Reference to bidirectional replication.

4. Reference to the daughter DNA molecule being attached to the cell surface membrane.

5. Reference to cell elongation causing the two chromosomes to separate.

6. Reference to assembly of the septum.

7. Reference to cell wall materials, that is peptidoglycan, being added.

Comparison with mitosis

8. Similarity: reference to separation of chromosomes.

9. Difference: reference to presence or absence of nuclear division.

10. Difference: reference to presence or absence of DNA replication.

11. Difference: reference to circular against linear chromosomes.

12. Difference: reference to disintegration of the nuclear envelope or the lack of it.

13. Difference: reference to movement of centrioles to opposite poles or the lack of it.

14. Difference: reference to condensation of chromosomes or the lack of it.

15. Difference: reference to attachment of microtubules to chromosomes or the lack of it.

16. Two further points credited on the same node elsewhere in the papers and worth adding. The bacterial chromosome has a single origin of replication, where a eukaryotic chromosome has many. And on septum formation, the cell membrane folds inwards, that is invaginates, to form a double layer across the long axis of the cell, with Reject: cell wall invaginates, cell invaginates printed beside it. The wall material is added afterwards, and saying it the wrong way round costs the mark.

Sources & concepts

Source: HCI Prelim 2021 P3 Q4(b), a Section B free-response essay, stem and key verbatim, at its real 10 marks. Marking point 16 is added from the YJC Prelim 2016 P2 Q10(a) and SAJC Prelim 2011 P2 Q3(b) keys, which set the same process and print the invagination reject, and is flagged as an addition rather than part of the HCI key. Archetype: the full-cycle process question. Book 4 essays are process-led, and this is one of the four rehearsed processes the whole Book's essay stock is built from: binary fission, plus a rider. Here the rider is mitosis. Trap: describing binary fission as mitosis without a spindle, when the scheme wants the membrane attachment, the single origin, the bidirectional replication and the septum stated positively; saying the cell wall invaginates, which is rejected by name; giving the comparison one-sidedly, so that only the bacterium is described; forgetting that DNA replication happens in both, which is one of the listed points and is a similarity people write as a difference. LOs: 2(g) outlining the mechanism of asexual reproduction by binary fission in a typical prokaryote, in full; 1(d) the structure of a typical bacterial cell, specifically circular DNA and the peptidoglycan wall. Reach-back to Book 3 for the stages of mitosis, the spindle, the centrioles and the nuclear envelope, and to Book 2 for semi-conservative replication and the origin of replication. Concepts fused: (1) chromosome anchored to the membrane; (2) semi-conservative replication; (3) a single origin; (4) bidirectional replication; (5) both daughter molecules anchored; (6) elongation as the separating force; (7) the septal ring and the septum; (8) membrane invagination; (9) new wall material added after; (10) chromosome separation as the shared outcome; (11) no nuclear division in a prokaryote; (12) circular against linear chromosomes; (13) no nuclear envelope to break down; (14) no centrioles and no spindle; (15) no condensation of chromosomes.

Question 4 [8 marks]

(a) Bacteria reproduce by the process of binary fission. Explain the significance of binary fission in bacteria. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain the significance of binary fission in bacteria. [2]

1. Reference to asexual reproduction for a unicellular organism.

2. Ensuring that offspring are genetically identical to the parent, that is desirable alleles or traits are passed down.

3. Rapid increase in cell numbers under favourable conditions.

4. Any 2.

(b) Bacteria reproduce asexually via binary fission to produce genetically identical daughter bacterial cells. Nevertheless, binary fission is considered one of the processes contributing to the extensive genetic variation in bacteria. Explain how binary fission contributes to the extensive genetic variation in bacteria. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain how binary fission contributes to the extensive genetic variation in bacteria. [2]

1. Mutation occurs, and

2. the short generation time, that is high rate of bacterial reproduction, allows any mutated DNA sequence to be propagated and accumulated quickly in a population.

3. Hold this apart from the standing statement that binary fission is unable to give rise to genetic variation in a bacterial population. Both are true once you separate transfer from variation: binary fission itself copies a genome faithfully, so it generates nothing new, but it multiplies whatever a mutation has already produced. Your chapter 4.2 states both on consecutive pages, on page 13 and page 14, and Specimen Paper 1 Question 12 turns on exactly this ambiguity.

(c) DH5α T1R is a laboratory strain of Escherichia coli bacteria that has a number of features that make it particularly useful for research. These features include:

1 low risk of causing infections in humans 2 lacks endonucleases that could degrade plasmids 3 can easily take up DNA from its external environment 4 resistant to infection by T1 phage.

A culture of DH5α T1R cells that contained an F plasmid conferring resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin was grown for several generations in nutrient broth containing ampicillin. A small volume of this culture of DH5α T1R cells was then inoculated into a large volume of sterile nutrient broth, containing all of the requirements for optimal bacterial growth and without ampicillin. After incubating at 37 °C for eight hours, the number of bacterial cells present had increased by a factor of more than 15 million. Most, but not all, of these cells were found to be ampicillin resistant when tested.

Which method of gene transfer from one bacterial cell to another is responsible for the enormous increase in the number of DH5α cells that were resistant to ampicillin? [1]

Abinary fission
Bconjugation
Ctransduction
Dtransformation
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Which method of gene transfer from one bacterial cell to another is responsible for the enormous increase in the number of DH5α cells that were resistant to ampicillin? [1] [INFERRED: the 9477 specimen papers ship without a mark scheme, and this key is genuinely contested. Do not drill it as though it were settled]

1. The question bank keys this B, conjugation, and tags that answer itself as inferred with no official key behind it. There is a strong case for A, binary fission. Both readings are defensible. What is not in doubt is the distinction the question is testing, which is vertical against horizontal gene transfer, so be able to argue either way from the stem.

(d) Explain your answer, saying for each of the four options what the stem tells you and whether it rules that option in or out. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Explain your answer, saying for each of the four options what the stem tells you and whether it rules that option in or out. [3] [INFERRED]

1. The case for A, binary fission. The original culture was grown in ampicillin, so every cell in it already carried the F plasmid. It was then inoculated into sterile broth, so no F- partner exists for a mating. The stated observation is that cell number rose more than 15 million-fold in eight hours, which is replication, and that "most, but not all" cells were resistant, which is the classic pattern of plasmid loss during growth without selection. Conjugation between two F+ cells does not occur efficiently.

2. The case for B, conjugation. The phrase "gene transfer from one bacterial cell to another" is the standard wording for horizontal transfer, and a prelim scheme elsewhere in the papers rejects binary fission outright on the ground that it "is cell division, not gene transfer between cells".

3. C, transduction, is ruled out by feature 4: the strain is resistant to infection by T1 phage, and the broth is sterile, so no phage vector is present to carry DNA between cells.

4. D, transformation, is ruled out despite feature 3. Feature 3 says the cells take up DNA easily, and feature 2 says they lack endonucleases that could degrade plasmids, which is what makes them useful in a laboratory. But the broth was sterile and contained no added DNA, so there is no naked DNA in the environment to take up.

5. So the eliminators are in the stem's own numbered list and in the word "sterile", and the argument comes down to whether "gene transfer" is being used loosely enough to include a cell passing its plasmid to its own daughters.

Sources & concepts

Source: SAJC Prelim 2017 P2 Q4(b), stem and key verbatim (a); CJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q8(d), stem and key verbatim (b), with marking point 3 added from the digest of the school's own chapter 4.2; 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Question 12 in full, verbatim from the official question paper (c); the follow-on wording in (d) is the drill's, and both arguments are taken from the Book 4 examiner's guide, which sets out the contested key in full. Archetype: applied MCQ with the options pre-eliminated by features listed in the stem, then a full audit. Not one of the four Book 4 items on the specimen Paper 1 is plain recall, and this one requires the stem's four numbered features to be read as eliminators. Trap: answering (a) and (b) with the same paragraph, when (a) is about faithful copying and (b) is about mutation being amplified by a short generation time; assuming any question containing the phrase "gene transfer" must mean a horizontal mechanism; missing that the broth is sterile, which is the single word that removes both transduction and transformation; treating the four listed features as background rather than as the eliminators they are. LOs: 2(g) binary fission, and how transformation, transduction and conjugation give rise to variation in prokaryotic genomes, in all four parts; vertical against horizontal gene transfer as the frame, in (c) and (d). Concepts fused: (1) asexual reproduction of a unicellular organism; (2) genetically identical daughters; (3) rapid population growth; (4) mutation as the source of novelty; (5) short generation time as the amplifier; (6) vertical against horizontal transfer; (7) plasmid loss without selection; (8) the need for an F- partner; (9) a phage vector as the requirement for transduction; (10) naked DNA in the environment as the requirement for transformation; (11) reading a stem's feature list as a set of eliminators.

Question 5 [5 marks]

Fig. 5.1 shows a classic experiment used to show that physical contact between bacterial cells is necessary for conjugation to happen. A student tried to replicate the experiment but did not get the result shown in Fig. 5.1. Instead, he observed a few bacterial colonies which are hybrids of strains A and B. Afterwards, he realised that he forgot to add in DNase when carrying out the experiment.

(a) Briefly describe the role of DNase in this experiment. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Briefly describe the role of DNase in this experiment. [1]

1. To digest naked DNA fragments.

(b) How does the lack of DNase in the experiment result in the growth of the hybrid bacterial colonies? [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) How does the lack of DNase in the experiment result in the growth of the hybrid bacterial colonies? [2]

1. Without the DNase, the naked DNA fragments from bacteria which have died may be taken up by the other strain via transformation.

2. DNA fragments will be small enough to cross over the filter.

(c) The student repeated the experiment, this time with DNase added. However, he continued to observe a few bacterial colonies which are hybrids of strains A and B. The student confirmed that the filter was undamaged and there was no cross contamination between bacterial strain A and B. Suggest how bacterial colonies which are hybrids of strains A and B could have been obtained in the repeated experiment. Explain your answer. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Suggest how bacterial colonies which are hybrids of strains A and B could have been obtained in the repeated experiment. Explain your answer. [2]

1. Transduction.

2. Bacteriophages are smaller than bacteria, so they can pass through the filter.

3. The logic of the whole item is worth holding: the filter removes cell-to-cell contact, so conjugation is impossible; DNase removes naked DNA, so transformation is impossible; what is left that is small enough to cross a filter and is not naked DNA is a phage, and that is transduction.

The Fig. 5.1 image is the real Fig. 8.1 from the CJC 2023 Paper 2 question paper. Archetype: predict and apply to a novel case. The classic Davis U-tube is handed to you as an experiment and the three transfer mechanisms have to be used as hypotheses to be eliminated, which is a completely different demand from describing them. Trap: naming conjugation in (c) because the stem's opening sentence is about conjugation, when the filter is precisely what rules it out; giving "DNase destroys DNA" for (a) without the word naked, which is what makes it transformation rather than anything else; forgetting in (b) that two separate marks are on offer, the mechanism and the size argument. Question 6 [11 marks]

Escherichia coli is a common human food contaminant. An E. coli strain carrying the aphA1 and aphA2 genes is resistant to the antibiotic kanamycin.

(a) Describe the conditions needed for aphA1 and aphA2 genes to be transferred to other E. coli cells by transformation. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Describe the conditions needed for aphA1 and aphA2 genes to be transferred to other E. coli cells by transformation. [3]

1. Recipient cells must be competent, that is they must secrete the competence factor.

2. DNA containing the aphA1 and aphA2 genes must be exogenous, that is present in the environment.

3. ATP must be available.

4. Any artificial conditions that enhance competence, for example heat shock or electroporation.

5. Any 3. Note that point 4 is credited here as a condition but that artificial transformation methods have no learning outcome of their own, so read them once and never drill them.

6. A scheme elsewhere credits fragments of foreign naked DNA and prints R: chromosomal DNA (this is too big), so say fragments.

(b) Describe generalised and specialised transduction. [8]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Describe generalised and specialised transduction. [8]

Generalised transduction, maximum 4

1. A virulent phage infects a bacterial cell and hydrolytic enzymes degrade the host bacterial chromosome into fragments.

2. A small fragment of the host cell's degraded DNA is improperly packaged within a capsid,

3. rather than the phage genome, due to an error during the viral particle assembly process.

4. When this phage attaches to or infects another bacterial cell, it will inject this foreign bacterial DNA into its new host,

5. and it may be integrated into the new host bacterial chromosome under the proper circumstances

6. via homologous recombination.

Specialised transduction, maximum 4

7. A temperate phage infects a bacterial cell and has its viral DNA genome integrated into the bacterial chromosome.

8. When the prophage viral DNA is excised from the chromosome,

9. it sometimes takes with it a small region of adjacent bacterial DNA due to improper excision.

10. These bacterial DNA are injected, along with the phage's genome, into the next host bacterial cell and

11. may be integrated into the new host bacterial chromosome under the proper circumstances

12. via homologous recombination.

13. Maximum 4 marks for generalised and maximum 4 marks for specialised.

14. The pairing has to be automatic, because schemes reject it in both directions. One prints "REJECT specialised transduction, because the phage is T4 and the genetic material is a random piece of bacterial genetic material", another prints "Reject specialised transduction, since the figure shows a lytic phage which usually facilitates generalised transduction", and a generalised-transduction key prints (R: lytic phage) and (R: lysogenic phage) where virulent and temperate are the wanted words. Virulent and lytic go with generalised; temperate and lysogenic go with specialised, and the phage type is what you write, not the cycle.

15. The single word that distinguishes them: generalised is random, because each portion of the bacterial genome has approximately the same probability of being transferred; specialised is adjacent, because only genes near the prophage insertion site can travel.

Sources & concepts

Source: ACJC Prelim 2021 P2 Q7(a), reprinted as HCI Topical 2021 STQ Q3(a), stem and key verbatim (a), with marking point 6 added from the transformation scheme quoted in the Book 4 examiner's guide; CJC Prelim 2016 P2 Q10(b), stem and key verbatim including both maxima (b), with marking points 14 and 15 added from the transduction schemes quoted in the same guide. Archetype: recall and describe a process, at essay scale. Transduction is 12.1% of in-scope records and transformation 8.0%. Trap: writing "lytic phage" and "lysogenic phage" where virulent and temperate are the wanted words; attaching generalised transduction to a temperate phage or specialised to a virulent one, which schemes reject in both directions; giving transformation as uptake of chromosomal DNA rather than of fragments of naked DNA; forgetting homologous recombination, which is the step that makes the transferred DNA heritable and without which there is transfer but no inheritance and therefore no variation. LOs: 2(g) how transformation and transduction give rise to variation in prokaryotic genomes, in (a) and (b); homologous recombination, in (b). Reach-back to Cluster 1 for the lytic and lysogenic cycles, the prophage and the prophage insertion site throughout (b). Concepts fused: (1) competence and competence factors; (2) exogenous naked DNA as the material; (3) energy requirement; (4) fragments rather than a whole chromosome; (5) host chromosome degraded in the lytic cycle; (6) mispackaging at assembly; (7) the defective phage; (8) injection into a second host; (9) homologous recombination in the recipient; (10) prophage integration in the lysogenic cycle; (11) imprecise excision; (12) adjacency to the insertion site; (13) random against adjacent as the whole distinction; (14) virulent against temperate as the wanted vocabulary.

Question 7 [9 marks]

Fig. 7.1 shows two bacterial cells, bacterium A and bacterium B, involved in process X. Fig. 7.2 shows a section of an electron micrograph of bacterium A in Fig. 7.1, with structure C labelled.

(a) Explain the role of structure C. [3]

Figure not recovered. Described from the source paper: Fig. 7.2, a section of an electron micrograph of the inside of bacterium A. Structure C is labelled, and it is a small circular DNA molecule lying free in the cytoplasm, separate from the much larger bacterial chromosome.
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain the role of structure C. [3]

1. The F plasmid of the donor cell contains several genes that promote its transfer to other cells, that is the tra genes.

2. These genes code for the protein subunits that assemble on the surface of the bacterial cell which form the sex pilus.

3. The sex pilus extends and attaches to a recipient cell like a grappling hook.

4. The sex pilus retracts and the 2 cells are pulled towards each other so that a temporary mating or conjugation bridge can be formed. The scheme spells the distinction out inside its own answer text: sex pilus is not the conjugation bridge.

5. The F plasmid also contains an origin of replication where DNA replication can initiate.

6. The F plasmid also contains oriT, whereby one strand of DNA can be transferred to the F- cell via the rolling circle mechanism.

7. The F plasmid may also contain beneficial genes such as antibiotic or xenobiotic resistance.

8. Points 6 and 7 are the ones to notice. Neither the rolling circle mechanism nor the origin of transfer appears anywhere in your chapter 4.2, and at least eight prelim schemes in the papers credit the rolling circle mechanism as a mark point, several credit oriT, and two credit the tra genes. This is the largest single gap between your notes and the schemes anywhere in Book 4, and it is a missing mark rather than a wrong one. Add the words.

(b) The kanamycin-resistant E. coli strain can transfer the aphA1 and aphA2 genes to non-kanamycin-resistant E. coli via other mechanisms, such as transduction and conjugation. Contrast conjugation and transduction. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Contrast conjugation and transduction. [3]

1. Conjugation transfers the F plasmid, whereas in transduction, in generalised transduction any gene fragment of the bacterial chromosome can be transferred, and in specialised transduction only the gene fragment adjacent to the prophage in the bacterial chromosome is transferred.

2. Conjugation involves a sex pilus, does not involve a phage in the transfer mechanism, and involves direct contact between bacterial cells, whereas transduction involves a phage, does not involve a sex pilus in the transfer mechanism, and does not involve direct contact between bacterial cells.

3. Conjugation involves no homologous recombination, whereas transduction involves homologous recombination in the recipient bacterium.

4. In conjugation the donor bacterium is not lysed, whereas in transduction the donor bacterium is lysed.

5. Any 3. Point 3 is true because Hfr is excluded from the syllabus: the F plasmid is not integrated into the recipient's chromosome, so nothing has to recombine.

(c) Discuss the potential benefit of conjugation in a population of bacteria. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Discuss the potential benefit of conjugation in a population of bacteria. [3]

1. The recipient bacteria can acquire new genes that

2. code for advantageous traits. Give an example to illustrate: antibiotic resistance, resistance to heavy metals, resistance to drugs, or the ability to utilise new metabolites.

3. Increase genetic variation in the bacterial population. Binary fission only results in genetically identical cells, and mutations are random and spontaneous, so they will not contribute significantly to genetic variation.

4. Reference to evolutionary fitness or selective advantage of bacteria, giving any one example: improve its ability to survive, colonise environments or exploit new nutrient sources; reproduce more successfully; compete more effectively with other bacteria.

5. Reference to the idea that with genetic variation in a population, the population as a whole may survive environmental changes if at least some of its members in each generation can cope effectively with new conditions, that is the long-term survival of the species.

6. A scheme elsewhere prints Reject "allows bacteria to have selective advantage / advantageous traits" without reference to gaining of advantageous genes, and another rejects genetic diversity, variety and variance where genetic variation is the wanted term. Start at the genes.

Question 8 [14 marks]

(a) Explain how viruses challenge the cell theory while prokaryotes and eukaryotes comply with the cell theory. [14]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Explain how viruses challenge the cell theory while prokaryotes and eukaryotes comply with the cell theory. [14]

The cell theory

1. All living things are composed of one or more cells.

2. The cell is the smallest unit of life.

3. All cells come from pre-existing cells.

How viruses challenge it

4. A virus challenges the cell theory in that it has living characteristics but it is acellular, that is not a cell.

5. It is not a cell as it is simpler or less complex in structure than a cell. Reject "smaller".

6. Living characteristic: it has its own genetic material or genome, in the form of DNA in a bacteriophage or RNA in influenza or HIV, which codes for viral proteins.

7. Living characteristic: they are able to reproduce in a host cell.

8. Living characteristic: they are also able to undergo mutation and evolve into new viral strains. Reject "adapt to".

9. Not a cell: it does not have cytoplasm or organelles.

10. Not a cell: it contains only a protein capsid and a genome, and a viral envelope in some cases.

11. Not a cell: it does not contain enzymes necessary for metabolism, replication, transcription or translation to take place.

How prokaryotes and eukaryotes comply

12. Even though single-celled, they still possess characteristics of life: able to respond to stimuli, reproduce, grow in size, carry out metabolic reactions and evolve.

13. Prokaryotic cells reproduce via binary fission to produce genetically identical daughter cells.

14. Eukaryotic cells reproduce via mitosis and cytokinesis, that is cell division for somatic cells, to produce genetically identical daughter cells.

15. Eukaryotes can also undergo meiosis and cytokinesis to produce gametes for sexual reproduction.

16. During sexual reproduction, fertilisation occurs where a zygote is formed which develops into a multicellular blastocyst.

17. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have cytoplasm and many cellular organelles inside them, surrounded by a cell surface membrane or plasma membrane.

18. Prokaryotes, that is bacteria, are usually unicellular or single-celled.

19. Eukaryotes could be unicellular or single-celled, or multicellular.

20. Note: membrane-bound organelles are only present in eukaryotic cells, not in prokaryotic ones.

21. Quality of written communication: 1 correct point from the cell theory, 2 correct points from viruses and 2 correct points from prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

22. The chapter's own closing line is the safest way to resolve the discussion rather than leaving it open: it is best to describe viruses as infectious particles which are active as the intracellular virus state, or inactive as the extracellular virion state, as opposed to living or non-living.

Sources & concepts

Source: ACJC Prelim 2023 P3 Q4(a), a Section B free-response essay, stem, key and quality of written communication line verbatim, at its real 14 marks. Marking point 22 is added from the digest of the school's own chapter 4.1 and is flagged as an addition rather than part of the ACJC key. Archetype: evaluate and discuss. Only 1.4% of in-scope records fall here and almost all of them sit on this node, but the papers set a 14-mark essay on it, and discuss is the only two-sided command word in Book 4. Trap: giving a list of things viruses do and stopping, when the shape is three statements each conceded and then qualified; writing "smaller" where "simpler or less complex" is wanted, which the scheme rejects by name; writing "adapt to" for evolution, also rejected; running the whole 14 marks on viruses and giving nothing on prokaryotes and eukaryotes, when the quality of written communication mark requires two points from each; forgetting that a virion is metabolically inert and that a new virion is never formed directly from a pre-existing virion. LOs: 1(a) the cell theory, in full; 1(f) how viruses challenge the cell theory and concepts of what is considered living; 1(d) the structure of a typical bacterial cell; 2(g) binary fission. Reach-back to Cluster 1 for everything about viruses and to Book 3 for mitosis, meiosis and fertilisation. Concepts fused: (1) the three statements of the cell theory; (2) acellularity as the core challenge; (3) simplicity rather than size as the wanted wording; (4) a genome coding for proteins as a living characteristic; (5) reproduction inside a host as a living characteristic; (6) mutation and evolution as a living characteristic; (7) absence of cytoplasm and organelles; (8) absence of metabolic enzymes; (9) prokaryotic compliance through binary fission; (10) eukaryotic compliance through mitosis; (11) meiosis and fertilisation; (12) cytoplasm and a cell surface membrane in both; (13) unicellular against multicellular; (14) the intracellular against extracellular resolution.

Question 9 [6 marks]

(a) Some strains of bacteria have become resistant to practically all of the commonly available antibiotics. A notorious case is methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). An old antibiotic, vancomycin, was resurrected for treatment of MRSA infections. Molecular studies revealed that a plasmid-borne transposable element encodes enzymes and regulator proteins that confer resistance of MRSA to the antibiotic vancomycin. Describe two ways by which vancomycin resistance may spread naturally amongst bacteria. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Describe two ways by which vancomycin resistance may spread naturally amongst bacteria. [2]

1. Transformation. Release of the plasmid containing the vancomycin resistance gene into the environment, and uptake of the plasmid by bacterial cells.

2. Conjugation. Contact between recipient F- and donor F+ cells, involving formation of a sex pilus, and transfer of the vancomycin resistance gene found on the F plasmid.

3. Transduction. The vancomycin resistance gene from the host or donor bacterium is transferred to the recipient bacterial cell via a bacteriophage, the donor DNA from the host being accidentally packaged within a viral capsid, and progeny phages infecting other bacteria.

4. Maximum 2.

5. A scheme elsewhere rejects binary fission where the stem says "spread naturally amongst bacteria", because that phrase implies horizontal transfer between cells and binary fission is vertical.

(b) Which row correctly describes the transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another? [1]

binary fissiontransductionconjugation
Abacterial chromosome and plasmids pass to daughter cellsDNA transferred by bacteriophage from one bacterium to anothersingle strand of F plasmid transferred from one bacterium to another
Bbacterial chromosome and plasmids pass to daughter cellsbacterial cell takes up foreign DNA from culture mediumdouble strand of F plasmid transferred from one bacterium to another
Conly plasmids pass to daughter cellsDNA transferred by bacteriophage from one bacterium to anothersingle strand of F plasmid transferred from one bacterium to another
Donly plasmids pass to daughter cellsbacterial cell takes up foreign DNA from culture mediumdouble strand of F plasmid transferred from one bacterium to another
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Which row correctly describes the transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another? [1]

1. The key is A.

(c) Explain your answer, saying for each of the three named processes which of the two descriptions offered is correct and why the other is wrong. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain your answer, saying for each of the three named processes which of the two descriptions offered is correct and why the other is wrong. [3] [INFERRED: the school's teacher copy gives the key only; reasoning cross-checked against the AJC Prelim 2014 P2 Q9(a), IJC Prelim 2018 P2 Q2(c) and DHS Prelim 2017 P1 keys, which set the same three descriptions]

1. Binary fission: "bacterial chromosome and plasmids pass to daughter cells" is correct, and "only plasmids pass to daughter cells" is wrong. In binary fission the bacterial chromosome is replicated semi-conservatively and one copy goes to each daughter cell, and any plasmid replicates independently from its own origin of replication and is also passed on, so both molecules travel.

2. Transduction: "DNA transferred by bacteriophage from one bacterium to another" is correct, and "bacterial cell takes up foreign DNA from culture medium" is wrong, because that description is transformation, which needs no vector at all.

3. Conjugation: "single strand of F plasmid transferred from one bacterium to another" is correct, and "double strand of F plasmid transferred" is wrong. One strand of the F plasmid is nicked by an endonuclease at oriT and the nicked single strand moves to the F- recipient through the mating bridge; the complementary strand is then synthesised in each cell, so what crosses the bridge is single-stranded and what ends up in each cell is double-stranded.

4. So row A is the only row correct on all three, and each wrong row is wrong because it has swapped in the description of a different process or halved what binary fission carries.

Archetype: applied recall and an audited table MCQ. The three transfer mechanisms compared in one question account for 8.3% of in-scope records, and this is the shape that comparison usually takes on Paper 1. Trap: naming binary fission as a way resistance spreads between bacteria, which a scheme rejects for exactly that stem wording; confusing transduction with transformation, which is the swap both wrong rows are built on; saying the whole double-stranded plasmid crosses to the recipient; forgetting that the recipient becomes F+ and can then act as a donor itself, which is what makes resistance spread so fast. LOs: 2(g) how transformation, transduction and conjugation give rise to variation in prokaryotic genomes, and binary fission, in (a), (b) and (c); vertical against horizontal gene transfer as the frame. Reach-back to Cluster 1 for the phage as vector and to Book 2 for semi-conservative replication in (c). Concepts fused: (1) plasmid release and uptake as transformation; (2) F+ to F- contact as conjugation; (3) mispackaging into a capsid as transduction; (4) horizontal against vertical transfer; (5) both chromosome and plasmid passing at binary fission; (6) independent plasmid replication; (7) a phage as an obligatory vector for transduction; (8) uptake from the medium as the mark of transformation; (9) the endonuclease nick at oriT; (10) single-stranded transfer with complementary synthesis in both cells.
